sudan.title: البرهان ومناوي.. خلاف ما قبل المفاصلة - صحيفة التغيير السودانية
sudan.summary: تتناول المقالة الخلافات المتزايدة بين قائد الجيش السوداني، عبد الفتاح البرهان، وزعيم حركة تحرير السودان، مني أركو مناوي، في ظل الأوضاع السياسية المتوترة في البلاد. يشير المقال إلى أن العلاقة بين الطرفين كانت قد شهدت تعاونًا في السابق، لكن الأحداث الأخيرة أدت إلى تصاعد التوترات. يتناول المقال أيضًا تأثير هذه الخلافات على المشهد السياسي في السودان، حيث يتوقع أن تؤثر على جهود السلام والاستقرار. كما يسلط الضوء على التحديات التي تواجهها الحكومة الانتقالية في ظل هذه الانقسامات، مما يزيد من تعقيد الوضع في البلاد.

sudan.title: وفاة 150 شخصاً بهجوم للجيش السوداني على سوق في أبيي - Sharjah24
sudan.summary: قُتل 150 شخصاً في هجوم شنه الجيش السوداني على سوق في منطقة أبيي. الهجوم، الذي وقع في وقت متأخر من يوم السبت، أسفر عن إصابة العديد من المدنيين وتدمير الممتلكات. وقد أدان المجتمع الدولي هذا الهجوم، مطالباً بوقف العنف وحماية المدنيين. تأتي هذه الأحداث في ظل تصاعد التوترات في المنطقة، حيث يعاني السكان من الأزمات الإنسانية والنزاعات المستمرة. يُعتبر هذا الهجوم من بين الأكثر دموية في الفترة الأخيرة، مما يزيد من القلق بشأن الوضع الأمني في السودان.

sudan.title: مرسوم سيادي يعدل 6 قوانين رئيسية بالسودان - سودان اندبندنت
sudan.summary: أصدر رئيس مجلس السيادة في السودان مرسوماً سيادياً يعدل ستة قوانين رئيسية، في خطوة تهدف إلى تحديث الإطار القانوني في البلاد. تشمل التعديلات قوانين تتعلق بالجرائم والعقوبات، وقانون الإجراءات الجنائية، وقانون الأحوال الشخصية، بالإضافة إلى قوانين أخرى ذات صلة. تأتي هذه التعديلات في سياق جهود الحكومة الانتقالية لتعزيز سيادة القانون وتحسين النظام القضائي. وقد تم الإعلان عن المرسوم في وقت تشهد فيه البلاد تحديات سياسية واقتصادية، مما يعكس رغبة الحكومة في تحقيق إصلاحات قانونية تساهم في استقرار السودان.

sudan.title: «يونيسف»: مقتل (12) طفلًا في هجمات على الخرطوم وغرب كردفان - سودان تربيون
sudan.summary: أعلنت منظمة الأمم المتحدة للطفولة "يونيسف" عن مقتل 12 طفلًا في هجمات شهدتها العاصمة السودانية الخرطوم وولاية غرب كردفان. وأكدت المنظمة أن الأطفال هم من بين الضحايا الذين سقطوا نتيجة تصاعد العنف في المنطقة. كما أعربت "يونيسف" عن قلقها العميق إزاء تأثير النزاع على الأطفال، مشددة على ضرورة حماية حقوقهم وتوفير الحماية اللازمة لهم. ودعت المنظمة المجتمع الدولي إلى اتخاذ إجراءات عاجلة لحماية الأطفال في مناطق النزاع وتقديم الدعم الإنساني للمتضررين.

sudan.title: السودان - الأمم المتحدة تدين هجمات المسيرات وتدعو إلى حماية المدنيين والبنية التحتية المدنية - UN News
sudan.summary: أدانت الأمم المتحدة الهجمات التي تشنها الطائرات المسيرة في السودان، مشددة على ضرورة حماية المدنيين والبنية التحتية المدنية. جاء ذلك في بيان رسمي، حيث أعربت المنظمة الدولية عن قلقها العميق إزاء تصاعد العنف وتأثيره على حياة السكان. ودعت جميع الأطراف المعنية إلى الالتزام بالقانون الدولي الإنساني وضمان سلامة المدنيين. كما أكدت الأمم المتحدة على أهمية اتخاذ تدابير فورية لحماية البنية التحتية الحيوية، مثل المستشفيات والمدارس، من أي اعتداءات.

sudan.title: السودان: ارتفاع عدد قتلى قصف سوق إلى أكثر من 150 قتيلاً - القدس العربي
sudan.summary: ارتفع عدد القتلى جراء قصف سوق في السودان إلى أكثر من 150 شخصًا، وفقًا لتقارير محلية. وقع الهجوم في منطقة نائية، حيث كان المدنيون يتجمعون لشراء احتياجاتهم. وقد أسفر القصف عن إصابة العديد من الأشخاص بجروح خطيرة، مما زاد من القلق بشأن الوضع الإنساني في البلاد. تأتي هذه الحادثة في وقت تعاني فيه السودان من صراعات مستمرة وأزمات إنسانية متفاقمة. وقد أدانت منظمات حقوق الإنسان الهجوم، داعية إلى تحقيق مستقل لمحاسبة المسؤولين. الوضع في السودان يتطلب استجابة عاجلة من المجتمع الدولي لتقديم المساعدة للمتضررين.

sudan.title: تقرير: 67% من الأسر في السودان تفتقر للمياه و53.7% لخدمات الصرف الصحي - سودان تربيون
sudan.summary: أفاد تقرير حديث أن 67% من الأسر في السودان تعاني من نقص في المياه، بينما 53.7% تفتقر إلى خدمات الصرف الصحي. يشير التقرير إلى أن هذه الأرقام تعكس أزمة حادة في البنية التحتية الأساسية، مما يؤثر سلباً على صحة السكان وجودة حياتهم. كما يسلط الضوء على التحديات التي تواجهها الحكومة في توفير هذه الخدمات الأساسية، في ظل الظروف الاقتصادية والسياسية الصعبة التي تمر بها البلاد. ويعتبر تحسين الوصول إلى المياه والصرف الصحي أمراً ضرورياً لتحقيق التنمية المستدامة وضمان رفاهية المواطنين.

sudan.title: اتهامات للجيش السوداني بشن غارات دامية على منطقة أبيي المتنازع عليها - جريدة القدس
sudan.summary: اتهمت مصادر محلية الجيش السوداني بشن غارات جوية على منطقة أبيي المتنازع عليها، مما أسفر عن سقوط عدد من القتلى والجرحى. وأفادت التقارير أن الغارات استهدفت مناطق سكنية، مما أثار قلق السكان المحليين ودفعهم إلى النزوح. تأتي هذه الأحداث في وقت حساس حيث تتصاعد التوترات بين السودان وجنوب السودان حول السيطرة على المنطقة الغنية بالموارد. وقد أدانت منظمات حقوقية الهجمات، داعية إلى تحقيق مستقل في الحوادث. الوضع في أبيي يظل متأزماً، حيث يسعى الطرفان إلى تعزيز مواقعهما في المنطقة.

sudan.title: مصر والسودان تنسقان لاحتواء تداعيات حادثي الدهابة والخرطوم.. مصادر تكشف تفاصيل تحركات جديدة - Arabicpost.net — عربي بوست
sudan.summary: تنسق مصر والسودان جهودًا لاحتواء تداعيات حادثي الدهابة والخرطوم، حيث تشير مصادر إلى تحركات جديدة بين البلدين. الحادثان، اللذان وقعا مؤخرًا، أسفرا عن توترات أمنية وقلق متزايد في المنطقة. تسعى الحكومتان إلى تعزيز التعاون الأمني وتبادل المعلومات لمواجهة التحديات المشتركة. كما تم التأكيد على أهمية الحوار بين الجانبين لضمان استقرار الأوضاع. تأتي هذه التحركات في إطار الجهود المستمرة لتعزيز العلاقات الثنائية وتحقيق الأمن الإقليمي.

sudan.title: تصاعد المطالبات بإقالة رئيس لجنة الأمل للعودة الطوعية من مصر ومحمد وداعة يرد - Radio Dabanga
sudan.summary: تصاعدت المطالبات بإقالة رئيس لجنة الأمل للعودة الطوعية من مصر، محمد وداعة، بسبب انتقادات تتعلق بإدارته للجنة. وقد أبدى عدد من الناشطين والمواطنين استياءهم من أداء اللجنة، معتبرين أنها لم تحقق الأهداف المرجوة في تسهيل عودة اللاجئين. في ردّه على هذه الانتقادات، أكد وداعة أن اللجنة تعمل بجد لتلبية احتياجات اللاجئين، مشيراً إلى التحديات التي تواجهها في هذا السياق. كما دعا إلى الحوار والتعاون بين جميع الأطراف المعنية لتحسين الوضع.

ethiopia.title: Prisoner of History, Not Geography
ethiopia.content: Ethiopia: Prisoner of History, Not Geography - allAfrica.com AllAfrica English (current) En Français Toggle navigation My Account Toggle navigation AllAfrica My Account English (current) En Français Ethiopia: Prisoner of History, Not Geography 20 October 2026 Addis Standard (Addis Ababa) opinion Addis Abeba — In early October 2026, Ethiopia and Eritrea took their quarrel to the UN Security Council by letter. Addis Abeba told council members that Eritrean troops had advanced up to 60 km into Tigray, which Eritrea denies. Asmara replied by calling the accusation a declaration of war and asking the council to take deterrent measures. Ethiopia also alleges that Eritrea is helping fund, mobilize, and direct armed groups in the north. Eritrea, for its part, says Addis Abeba is using its demand for sea access, along with the refrain that Ethiopia "cannot remain a prisoner of geography," as a pretext for military escalation. Officially, Ethiopia says it would pursue access through peace and dialogue. Beneath the exchange of letters lies a misunderstanding of geopolitical theory. When leaders frame Ethiopia, a country of more than 120 million people, as trapped in a landlocked cell by an accident of nature, they borrow shorthand from Tim Marshall's best-selling Prisoners of Geography . It is the kind of snappy line that makes a regional crisis sound like spatial fate. It is a compelling narrative, but it misreads physical geography. Ethiopia's landlocked condition is historical, legal, and political . That is not semantic pedantry; it dictates the cure. If a state is trapped by nature, only brute force or miraculous engineering can break its walls. If it is trapped by human choices, then diplomacy, international law, and regional trade corridors are the proper keys. What a "Prisoner of Geography" actually means Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn Marshall's framework applies to immutable physical constraints: terrain that cannot be flattened, climates that cannot be negotiated with, and distances that cannot be erased. Russia is the classic case. Russia's western frontier rests on the North European Plain, a vast flat corridor from Germany to Moscow with no mountain range to stop an invader. Napoleon crossed it in 1812; Hitler in 1941. That vulnerability has driven centuries of Russian effort to push buffer zones westward. On the water, Russia has thousands of miles of coastline but few useful outlets. Murmansk stays ice-free but is hemmed in by the Greenland-Iceland-UK gap. The Black Sea fleet must pass through the Turkish-controlled Bosporus. The Baltic exits squeeze through the Danish straits, and Vladivostok is ice-affected in winter and tucked behind the Japanese archipelago. Catherine the Great's drive to the Black Sea answered this problem, and the problem has outlived her. Whether ruled by a Tsar, a Soviet commissar, or a modern president, the Kremlin keeps getting handed the same geography exam, and the water questions never get easier. This gives us a diagnostic test: a true prisoner of geography remains imprisoned no matter how many times the regime changes, the ideology shifts, or treaties are signed. Consider the rivers of Sub-Saharan Africa. The Congo and the Zambezi carry immense volumes of water, yet rapids, cataracts, and steep escarpments break them into disconnected stretches, preventing continuous navigation from the interior to the sea. Europe's navigable rivers carried goods straight to its ports. No act of parliament or diplomatic summit can persuade a waterfall to flow upstream. Applying the test to Ethiopia Ethiopia fails the test. Its topography is formidable: a volcanic highland massif carved by gorges and split by the Great Rift Valley, which made internal transport a historical challenge. But access to the Red Sea is a different spatial question. The coast is not separated from the highlands by impassable barriers, and Ethiopia has used it. Ethiopia's access to the sea has always been a matter of arrangements, not terrain. It reached the water first by the Franco-Ethiopian railway to Djibouti, which arrived in Addis Abeba in 1917, then, after the 1952 federation with Eritrea, through Assab and Massawa. Even after independence in 1993, cargo kept moving through Assab until the 1998-2000 war closed it. The land never changed. The paperwork did. Ethiopia's access to the sea has always been a matter of arrangements, not terrain." Ethiopia did not lose its coast because tectonic plates threw a tantrum or a mountain range erupted overnight. It lost the sea because of politics , the one force that can relocate a border faster than continental drift. The chain of events is long: Ottoman and Egyptian expansion along the coast; Italian colonization and the creation of Eritrea as a distinct unit; the 1952 UN federation ; the 1962 annexation under Emperor Haile Selassie; a thirty-year war of independence; the 1993 referendum ; and the breakdown of relations in 1998. Every link was a human decision. When Eritrea became independent, Assab became a foreign port, not because the earth shifted but because of a referendum that Ethiopia's own transitional government agreed to and the international community recognized. Ethiopia is not a prisoner of geography. It is a prisoner of history. Global Lessons: Bolivia, Switzerland, and international law The distinction between historical contingency and geographic destiny is well illustrated elsewhere. Bolivia lost its Pacific coastline to Chile in the War of the Pacific in the 1880s. Like Ethiopia, it became landlocked through a lost war and later treaties, not because a mountain range rose between its cities and the sea. Bolivia still marks a Day of the Sea each year and keeps a navy on Lake Titicaca, a remarkable act of national memory. Yet when it took Chile to the International Court of Justice , the court ruled in 2018 that Chile had no obligation to negotiate sovereign access. Bolivia's practical economic life has gone on through transit corridors and port facilities on the Chilean and Peruvian coasts. Switzerland, an Alpine nation with no coast, moves its exports down the Rhine to Rotterdam under negotiated transit arrangements with its neighbors. The pattern is clear: where landlocked status is the product of history and borders, commercial access is solved through law, diplomacy, and shared infrastructure, not by claiming a neighbor's territory. International law reflects this. Article 125 of the 1982 UN Convention on the Law of the Sea guarantees landlocked states a right of access to and from the sea and freedom of transit. It grants a right of transit, not a right to a sovereign coastline. The danger of misdiagnosis Misdiagnosing a political problem as geographic destiny is a dangerous policy mistake. If a nation convinces itself that it sits in a permanent cage imposed by nature, peaceful tools start to look inadequate, and force starts to look like liberation. To be fair to Addis Abeba, Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed describes the quest for sea access as irreversible while stressing his commitment to diplomacy. But rhetoric about spatial entitlement has a way of outrunning the diplomacy it promises. The 1998-2000 war killed tens of thousands, devastated both economies, and ended with Ethiopia cut off from Assab, the opposite of its intended effect. Critics will say that Eritrea's own secession shows borders do change. They do, and the difference is consent. Eritrea's independence came through a referendum that Ethiopia's government accepted. Taking a port by force would set a different precedent: that population size or historical grievance justifies redrawing sovereign boundaries. On a continent whose borders were largely drawn by colonial cartographers, that principle would threaten the foundations of the African Union and, in time, Ethiopia's own boundaries. The alternatives are practical, if imperfect. Djibouti handles most of Ethiopia's trade, and diversifying through Berbera, Lamu, and Port Sudan would reduce dependence on it. Each comes with caveats: Berbera lies in Somaliland, whose status Somalia contests, and Port Sudan sits in a country at war. The strongest option is a negotiated commercial arrangement with Eritrea itself, such as port-use rights, shared infrastructure, and trade guarantees, built on the Algiers Agreement framework that both sides signed in 2000. Over-reliance on one corridor through Djibouti burdens Ethiopian businesses, creates strategic vulnerability and constrains a giant economy. Acknowledging that does not require mislabeling its cause. Russia cannot negotiate away the flat open corridor of the North European Plain, and African inland states cannot treaty away river cataracts. Ethiopia can negotiate, build, and trade its way to secure, diversified sea access. Geology may even help eventually: the Afar rift is slowly pulling Africa apart, and some geologists expect a new sea to form there in millions of years. Diplomacy is faster. Ethiopia is not locked in a natural prison. The cell was built by human history, and its door can be opened by human diplomacy. Conclusion The "prisoner of geography" narrative inherently invites military solutions, tempting leaders to enforce their will through force rather than diplomacy. Yet, territory and seaports seized at the barrel of a gun cannot deliver long-term security. True statesmanship lies in converting battlefield leverage into lasting political settlements before war becomes inevitable. Negotiation must not be a desperate last resort pursued only when ammunition is spent, and the economy has collapsed--as the Derg regime learned far too late after squandering its golden opportunities for peace. Real military maturity is measured by using power to forge peace while strong. As Scripture reminds us to remember our Creator in our youth, the optimal time to secure the Horn of Africa's future is during moments of strength. Ethiopia alleges Eritrea is supporting armed groups in the north, while Eritrea accuses Ethiopia of using its landlocked status as a pretext for military action. ethiopia.title: News - 13-Year-Old Girl Killed After Flag Dispute in Borana's Moyale - Protesters Block Transport Services
ethiopia.content: Ethiopia: News - 13-Year-Old Girl Killed After Flag Dispute in Borana's Moyale - Protesters Block Transport Services - allAfrica.com AllAfrica English (current) En Français Toggle navigation My Account Toggle navigation AllAfrica My Account English (current) En Français Ethiopia: News - 13-Year-Old Girl Killed After Flag Dispute in Borana's Moyale - Protesters Block Transport Services 20 October 2026 Addis Standard (Addis Ababa) Addis Abeba — The opening of a new Somali Region administration office and the raising of its flag in Moyale town in Borana zone of Oromia regional state on October 18 triggered an exchange of gunfire between Somali regional forces and Oromia local militias, leaving a 13-year-old girl dead and prompting protests that disrupted transport services and forced businesses to close on Monday, residents told Addis Standard . Residents who spoke to Addis Standard accuse the Somali Region Police of shooting at the child and killing her instantly. Meanwhile, residents from the Somali side told Addis Standard that the girl was killed in crossfire between the two sides. Following the incident, elders and security officials reportedly agreed on Monday to remove the Somali Region's flag. However, the decision prompted demonstrations by Somali resident particularly in Kebele 02 on Tuesday that disrupted transport services and forced businesses and bus stations to close amid security fears. Mallicha Diida, a resident of Moyale's Kebele 02, told Addis Standard that the latest incident was part of a recurring cycle of violence in the town. Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn "In Moyale, human blood has been spilled year after year. Last Sunday, when Somali Regional administration bodies opened a new mayor's office around Kebele 02 and hoisted the Somali Region flag, this act deeply angered many people," he said. Mallicha said gunfire subsequently broke out between Oromia militia members and Somali Region police, prompting the immediate intervention of the Ethiopian National Defense Force (ENDF), which stopped the exchange. He alleged that Somali Region police shot and killed the 13-year-old girl, describing the incident as an act of "cruelty and lawlessness". He said the officers had killed the child rather than hold those responsible for any alleged wrongdoing accountable, claiming they accused her of throwing stones at them. A resident on the Somali side offered a different account, telling Addis Standard that the Somali-side Moyale town administration had merely relocated its office from its previous premises to a new location. "When they attempted to bring office equipment and hoist the flag, Oromia Region militias opened fire on the Somali Region police to prevent them from succeeding. The young girl was killed in the middle of this, but Somali Region security forces did not target or kill that child," the resident said, rejecting allegations that Somali Region forces were responsible for her death. However, a security official who spoke to Addis Standard said Somali Region security forces killed the 13-year-old in connection with the dispute over the flag. The official said the two sides exchanged gunfire for several minutes before the ENDF intervened and halted the shooting. Shuraa Waariyoo, the girl's uncle, identified her as Diqqoo Jaataan Aagaa and said her body had not been buried as of Tuesday. He alleged that Somali Region forces had taken the body following the killing and said the family was still in discussions with the relevant authorities to secure its return. Security forces from both sides and the ENDF held discussions following the incident. However, the security official told Addis Standard that the talks failed to produce an agreement. Moyale has repeatedly experienced clashes linked to territorial disputes between Borana communities in Oromia and Garre communities in the Somali Region, resulting in deaths, displacement and the burning of residents' homes. Tensions intensified in July and August 2025 after the Somali Regional State approved an administrative restructuring plan that created new woredas and zonal administrations, drawing protests and criticism from Oromo opposition parties over changes affecting contested territories. Subsequent clashes along the Oromia-Somali border killed residents and displaced more than 288,000 people. Read the original article on Addis Standard . ethiopia.title: Court News: High-Level Ethiopian Ministry Officials and Associates Charged in Over 1.1 Billion Birr Corruption and Money Laundering Scheme - EthiopiaToday
ethiopia.summary: High-level officials from the Ethiopian Ministry of Finance and their associates have been charged in connection with a corruption and money laundering scheme involving over 1.1 billion Birr. The charges stem from allegations of embezzlement and misappropriation of public funds, with the accused reportedly diverting significant amounts of money intended for government projects. The investigation, led by the Federal Ethics and Anti-Corruption Commission, uncovered a network of fraudulent activities that exploited the ministry's financial systems. The case highlights ongoing concerns about corruption within the Ethiopian government and the efforts to hold accountable those involved in such illicit practices. The accused individuals face serious legal repercussions as the case progresses through the judicial system.

This development highlights a shift in regional alliances and reflects Israel's growing diplomatic engagement with African nations. The map aims to strengthen ties with these countries amid ongoing geopolitical changes in the region. The implications of this map could affect Israel's relationships with neighboring countries and its strategic interests in Africa.

ethiopia.title: PM Abiy Says Eritrean People Have Lost Former Assets Since Secession
ethiopia.content: Ethiopia: PM Abiy Says Eritrean People Have Lost Former Assets Since Secession - allAfrica.com AllAfrica English (current) En Français Toggle navigation My Account Toggle navigation AllAfrica My Account English (current) En Français Ethiopia: PM Abiy Says Eritrean People Have Lost Former Assets Since Secession 20 October 2026 Ethiopian News Agency (Addis Ababa) Addis Ababa — Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed said Eritrean people have lost much of its industrial capacity and urban vitality since secession, urging good neighborliness and development cooperation as the path forward. During an interview with the Ethiopian Broadcasting Corporation (EBC), the Prime Minister said Eritrean cities were once thriving economic centers when Eritrea was part of Ethiopia. However, these assets have significantly deteriorated since Eritrea's secession, with some cities losing much of their former urban character. Follow us on WhatsApp | LinkedIn for the latest headlines Recalling that Eritrea had more than 300 industries during that period, the Premier said the region had a substantial industrial base, contrasting its former economic strength with what he described as its present decline. Citing Asmara, PM Abiy said the capital had become smaller than many developing Ethiopian cities such as Arba Minch and Jigjiga. Speaking about the Red Sea port cities of Massawa and Assab, the Prime Minister said their economic activity had declined significantly, leaving their potential largely underutilized. "Massawa has been emptied, while Assab has been reduced to a ghost town," Prime Minister Abiy said. The Prime Minister attributed the situation to the Eritrean government's failure to prioritize development and institution-building, adding that its policies had instead drawn the country into serving the interests of forces opposed to Ethiopia. He said Eritreans, whom he described as industrious and welcoming, were now facing displacement and hardship, underscoring that external factors supporting confrontation would not resolve the country's underlying challenges. Such involvement, the Premier said, offers no lasting solution to Eritrea's problems, as those supporting confrontation are more likely to provide ammunition than contribute to addressing the country's difficulties. He stressed that friendship, good neighborliness and development cooperation remain the viable path forward, noting that decades of experience have demonstrated the limitations of alternative approaches. The Prime Minister warned that continued disregard for calls to pursue partnership and development, rather than allowing the region to become an arena for external rivalries, could have serious consequences. ethiopia.title: Eritrea's Migration Economy - Can the Nation Survive Without Forced Remittance?
ethiopia.content: Eritrea's Migration Economy - Can the Nation Survive Without Forced Remittance? - allAfrica.com AllAfrica English (current) En Français Toggle navigation My Account Toggle navigation AllAfrica My Account English (current) En Français Eritrea's Migration Economy - Can the Nation Survive Without Forced Remittance? 20 October 2026 Ethiopian News Agency (Addis Ababa) October 20, 2026 (ENA) Britain's October 2026 ultimatum to Eritrea exposed a long-standing contradiction at the heart of Isaias Afwerki's regime. The Asmara administration promotes self-reliance while rejecting fixed national budgets and external dependence. Yet, its system is sustained by the very forces it claims to transcend: indefinite national service drives emigration, while remittances from Eritreans abroad help finance the system that compels them to leave. Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood announced that Eritrea faces a total visa ban for its nationals unless Asmara resumes cooperation on the return of failed asylum seekers and foreign national offenders. Preferential processing for officials has already been withdrawn, and diplomats have been placed under travel limits outside London. This announcement came at a moment when Eritreans formed the largest nationality among small-boat arrivals in the year to June 2026--roughly 5,875 recorded arrivals, or about 18 percent of the total--and ranked second in overall asylum claims, with initial grant rates near 83-84 percent. Although Eritrea dismissed the pressure as a "dismissible political gimmick," the sequence of events requires a closer examination of a political economy that has organized continuous emigration into a remittance resource. Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn That political economy, controlled by Shabia under President Isaias Afwerki since independence, rests on three interlocking pillars: indefinite national service, party ownership of the command economy, and the systematic capture of external financial flows. While appearing distinct, these pillars function as a single mechanism that converts the population into both a captive labor force at home and a source of finance abroad. This framework structured itself around the continuous extraction of value from that emigration, yielding a sustained regime monopoly. Way back in 1997, Eritrea ratified a constitution that has remained unimplemented for nearly three decades. In 2001, independent media outlets were shut down after senior party figures called for democratic elections and constitutional enforcement. As a result, what was once framed as temporary wartime mobilization hardened into a permanent state architecture in which citizenship itself was redefined as an obligation rather than a right. Although national service was formally limited to 18 months under Proclamation 82/1995, it has operated without an end date since the 1998-2000 border war. Secondary school students complete their final year at the Sawa military training center before being assigned to military or civilian roles that can last for decades, earning a meager stipend of 450 to 500 Nakfa a month--roughly 30 USD. Conditions like these are what the UN Commission of Inquiry characterized as "slavery-like," linking them to arbitrary detention and the collective punishment of families. Such practices drive continuous emigration, where the outflow is not a policy failure but rather a deliberate revenue stream. While resident population estimates hover around 3.6 million, diaspora figures range from roughly 600,000 to 900,000 registered migrants and refugees, with up to one-third of the Eritrean-born population living outside the country. According to UNHCR data for the end of 2025, there were roughly 555,000 refugees plus more than 118,000 asylum seekers--totaling approximately 670,000-679,000 people of concern--with new asylum applications in 2025 alone exceeding 53,000. Although the formal economy remains dominated by Shabia-linked enterprises and the state, private-sector activity outside small family trade is constrained by currency controls, licensing restrictions, and the national-service labor regime. The decisive resource is human capital exported and then taxed; most household survival depends on external transfers estimated at 200 to 300 million USD annually--equivalent to roughly 30 percent of Eritrea's GDP. These flows keep households solvent in an environment of limited domestic opportunity, while a parallel 2 percent diaspora tax is levied on Eritreans abroad and collected through embassies and informal networks. Economic ownership is concentrated in party-controlled structures: the Hidri Trust functions as the central holding vehicle for Shabia's commercial interests, the Red Sea Trading Corporation holds an effective monopoly on significant imports and serves as a primary channel for foreign exchange, construction firms such as Segen and Bidho execute major works frequently using national-service labor, and Himbol Financial Services manages remittances and related transactions. State banks exist, yet the party retains parallel financial channels outside conventional budgetary oversight, amidst no comprehensive national budget having been published since independence. This dual extraction reduces the need for productive employment creation and creates a closed loop in which indefinite national service and political controls generate flight, which in turn generates remittances and state revenue. When compared to the official doctrine of self-reliance that Eritrea follows--which rejects aid dependency while treating citizens as both free labor and external financiers--isolation from conventional multilateral finance is justified, while political pluralism is framed as a threat to national unity and sovereignty. This produces a distinctive equilibrium in which political power is monopolized, and the regime's authority on budgets and the precise size of party holdings stay outside public scrutiny. Eritrea's political economy has converted a significant fraction of its population into a transnational resource, where labor is extracted under coercive conditions while the diaspora supplies foreign exchange, producing an equilibrium of repression and economic stagnation. Consequently, host states are left to absorb the social and fiscal costs, as the ruling Shabia system externalizes those costs while capturing the financial returns. Eritrea's migration economy is therefore not an unintended by-product of isolation, but the operating logic of a political order that converts its people into the principal resource keeping the regime intact. The stakes are the continuous depletion of a generation and the durability of a closed regime that feeds on it. Read the original article on ENA . ethiopia.summary: Eritrea's economy heavily relies on remittances from its diaspora, driven by a system of indefinite national service that compels emigration. The Eritrean government, led by President Isaias Afwerki, promotes self-reliance while simultaneously depending on financial flows from citizens abroad, which are crucial for the regime's survival. A recent ultimatum from the UK threatens visa bans unless Eritrea cooperates on returning failed asylum seekers, highlighting the contradiction in its policies. The regime's control over the economy, characterized by party ownership and a lack of a comprehensive national budget, perpetuates a cycle of repression and economic stagnation. As a result, Eritrea's migration economy is not merely a consequence of isolation but a fundamental aspect of its political structure, with significant implications for both the nation and its diaspora.

ethiopia.title: Ethiopia Signs Second-Phase LNG Development Deal for Ogaden Gas Field
ethiopia.content: Ethiopia Signs Second-Phase LNG Development Deal for Ogaden Gas Field - allAfrica.com AllAfrica English (current) En Français Toggle navigation My Account Toggle navigation AllAfrica My Account English (current) En Français Ethiopia Signs Second-Phase LNG Development Deal for Ogaden Gas Field 20 October 2026 Addis Standard (Addis Ababa) Addis Abeba — Chinese companies GCL Group and Jurong Group have signed an agreement to develop the second phase of a liquefied natural gas (LNG) project at Ethiopia's Calub gas field in the Somali Region, as the government seeks to expand commercial use of the country's natural gas reserves. The agreement, signed on 16 October at the Ministry of Mines in Addis Abeba in the presence of Mines Minister Alemtsehay Paulos, covers engineering, construction and natural gas liquefaction and processing services. It follows a strategic cooperation framework signed by the two companies in May 2026 and the commissioning of the project's first phase in October 2025. According to Seetao, the first phase consists of a modular LNG facility designed to process 200,000 cubic metres of natural gas daily, producing approximately 50,000 metric tonnes of LNG annually, primarily for domestic industrial consumers. The second phase is intended to increase production and serve international markets, although the companies have not disclosed the contract value, additional processing capacity or completion timeline. The agreement comes amid renewed efforts to commercialise the Ogaden Basin's gas resources after years of delays. In March 2026, GCL and Dangote Group signed a reported $4.2 billion , 25-year gas supply agreement for a urea fertiliser complex in Gode, with plans to transport gas from Calub through a pipeline of approximately 108-110 kilometres. Follow us on WhatsApp | LinkedIn for the latest headlines Poly-GCL, associated with GCL's wider corporate group, has operated in the basin since 2013 under production-sharing agreements covering the Calub and Hilala fields. Ethiopia's government terminated the company's contracts in September 2022 following disputes over capital registration, outstanding fees and delays in development, before reversing the decision in June 2024. In August 2022, Ethiopia received its first gas reserves certificate, confirming an estimated seven trillion cubic feet of natural gas in the Ogaden Basin, according to a study by Netherland, Sewell & Associates. Despite the renewed investment push, export arrangements for the LNG project remain unclear. Ethiopia is landlocked, and earlier proposals to transport gas to Djibouti for export have not resulted in a publicly confirmed export route for the second phase. The agreement's financing, delivery schedule and intended international buyers have also not been announced. Read the original article on Addis Standard . ethiopia.title: PM Abiy Warns Eritrea of 'Extremely Severe' Consequences If It Rejects Peace Call
ethiopia.content: Ethiopia: PM Abiy Warns Eritrea of 'Extremely Severe' Consequences If It Rejects Ethiopia's Peace Call Amid Rising Tensions - allAfrica.com AllAfrica English (current) En Français Toggle navigation My Account Toggle navigation AllAfrica My Account English (current) En Français Ethiopia: PM Abiy Warns Eritrea of 'Extremely Severe' Consequences If It Rejects Ethiopia's Peace Call Amid Rising Tensions 20 October 2026 Addis Standard (Addis Ababa) Addis Abeba — Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed has warned Eritrea of "extremely severe" consequences if its government continues to reject Ethiopia's calls for peace and regional cooperation, accusing Asmara of aligning itself with forces seeking to destabilize Ethiopia. He also called on Tigrayan youth to abandon armed struggle, accusing Tigrayan People's Liberation Front (TPLF) leaders of prolonging conflict at the expense of the region's population. In a Tigrigna-language interview with the Ethiopian Broadcasting Corporation (EBC), Abiy said Eritrea should pursue economic development and cooperation with Ethiopia rather than serve as a haven for forces hostile to the country. "Rather than becoming a development partner, choosing to be a haven for enemies is not beneficial; ignoring our call for peace, however, will carry extremely severe consequences," he said. Abiy criticized Eritrea's economic conditions, contrasting the country's present state with its industrial and commercial activity before independence. He claimed that Asmara had diminished in stature, Massawa remained in ruins, and Assab had become a wasteland, arguing that Eritrea's population had lost much of what it gained after independence. Follow us on WhatsApp | LinkedIn for the latest headlines He accused Eritrea's ruling People's Front for Democracy and Justice (PFDJ), which he referred to as Shaebia, of prioritizing regional destabilization over domestic development. He maintained that Ethiopia remained committed to peace and joint development but warned that continued rejection of its appeals would have serious consequences. The remarks come amid heightened tensions between Ethiopia and Eritrea, alongside renewed fighting and political uncertainty in northern Ethiopia. Relations between the two countries have deteriorated amid disagreements over regional security and Ethiopia's pursuit of access to the Red Sea. Addressing the situation in Tigray, Abiy said the federal government would support the region's reconstruction, lasting peace, and economic recovery. He urged residents to protect their institutions and work with federal and regional security structures until an elected administration is established through a free and democratic vote. He called on Tigrayan youth involved in armed movements to lay down their weapons and enter the disarmament, demobilization, and reintegration (DDR) process. He also urged military and political leaders to surrender peacefully, saying, "Enough is enough; peace is better." Abiy accused TPLF leaders of sending young people to fight while their families live abroad or in Addis Abeba and they accumulate wealth. He contrasted their circumstances with those of young Tigrayans who, he said, have suffered death, physical disabilities, and psychological trauma from successive rounds of fighting. ethiopia.title: Ethiopia's Abiy Urges Investment in Youth As Kenya Honors National Heroes
ethiopia.content: Kenya: Ethiopia's Abiy Urges Investment in Youth As Kenya Honors National Heroes - allAfrica.com AllAfrica English (current) En Français Toggle navigation My Account Toggle navigation AllAfrica My Account English (current) En Français Kenya: Ethiopia's Abiy Urges Investment in Youth As Kenya Honors National Heroes 20 October 2026 Capital FM (Nairobi) By Phidel Kizito Nairobi — Ethiopian Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed has called for greater investment in young people, saying Kenya's next phase of development will depend on its ability to turn freedom into economic opportunities for the next generation. Speaking during the Mashujaa Day celebrations in Eldoret, Uasin Gishu County, Abiy said the country's legacy of national heroes should inspire efforts to create jobs, strengthen public institutions and equip young people to shape the country's future. He said the meaning of freedom extended beyond the sacrifices made during the struggle for independence, requiring successive generations to translate those gains into opportunities for citizens. "Freedom is a trust we pass to the next generation, and we must turn it into opportunities for every citizen," Abiy said. Follow us on WhatsApp | LinkedIn for the latest headlines "Today's heroes include teachers, nurses, artists, athletes and people who create jobs. The message to young people is clear: you too can help build Kenya," he added. Abiy's remarks placed young people at the center of Kenya's development agenda, at a time when employment creation, enterprise growth and access to economic opportunities remain important policy priorities. Kenya's youth population presents both an opportunity for economic expansion and a challenge for policymakers, particularly as young people seek formal employment, financing for businesses and pathways into productive sectors of the economy. The Ethiopian leader said building successful nations required patience and investment in institutions capable of serving citizens, while giving young people the support needed to shape their futures. His remarks underscored the role of education, public service, entrepreneurship and creative industries in national development, broadening the definition of heroism beyond those recognized for political and historical contributions. Mashujaa Day, observed annually on October 20, honors Kenyans who have contributed to the country's independence, development and public life. The celebrations in Eldoret brought together national leaders and other invited dignitaries to recognize individuals whose contributions have helped shape Kenya. His comments sparked backlash, with critics accusing him of promoting xenophobia and racism. Omar, a Somali-American and one of the first Muslim women elected to Congress, has previously faced similar attacks from Trump and other political figures. The remarks have reignited discussions about immigration, race, and the treatment of minority lawmakers in the U.S. political landscape.

The commission has outlined the qualifications and criteria for the candidates, emphasizing the importance of transparency and fairness in the electoral process. The leadership elections in Galmudug are crucial for the region's stability and governance, and the commission aims to ensure that the elections are conducted smoothly. The Irish government and relevant agencies are working to investigate the situation and provide support to the affected children. This alarming situation highlights ongoing issues related to human trafficking and the need for enhanced protective measures for vulnerable minors.

somalia.summary: The National Sports Authority (NSA) is seeking full approval from the Central Affairs Committee (CAF) for the Essipong Stadium in preparation for an upcoming fixture involving the Somalia national football team. somalia.title: Somalia Receives 220 Citizens Repatriated From Yemen - Dawan Africa
somalia.summary: Somalia has welcomed back 220 of its citizens who were repatriated from Yemen. The returnees arrived at Mogadishu's Aden Adde International Airport, where they were received by government officials and representatives from the International Organization for Migration (IOM). Many of the repatriated individuals had faced difficult conditions in Yemen, prompting their return to Somalia. The government expressed its commitment to supporting the reintegration of these citizens into society, providing them with necessary assistance and resources. This repatriation effort is part of a broader initiative to ensure the safety and well-being of Somali nationals abroad.

football.title: الهلال السوداني يدعم صفوفه بصفقة متميزة في ختام الميركاتو - winwin
football.summary: أعلن نادي الهلال السوداني عن إتمام صفقة متميزة لتعزيز صفوف الفريق في ختام فترة الانتقالات الصيفية. حيث تمكن النادي من التعاقد مع لاعب جديد يُعتبر إضافة قوية للفريق، مما يعكس استراتيجية الهلال في تحسين الأداء والتنافس في البطولات المقبلة. يأتي هذا التعاقد في إطار سعي النادي لتحقيق نتائج إيجابية في الموسم الجديد، ويُتوقع أن يُحدث اللاعب تأثيرًا ملحوظًا في تشكيلة الفريق.

football.title: الهلال السوداني يعلن وصول السوباط إلى كيغالي - سودان اندبندنت
football.summary: أعلن نادي الهلال السوداني عن وصول مدربه الجديد، السوباط، إلى العاصمة الرواندية كيغالي. تأتي هذه الزيارة في إطار استعدادات الفريق للمشاركة في البطولات المقبلة. السوباط، الذي تم تعيينه مؤخرًا، يسعى لتعزيز أداء الفريق وتحقيق نتائج إيجابية. يترقب مشجعو الهلال ما سيقدمه المدرب من تغييرات واستراتيجيات جديدة خلال الفترة القادمة.

football.title: حرب تصريحات.. الهلال السوداني يرد على رئيس اتحاد الكرة! - winwin
football.summary: الهلال السوداني رد على تصريحات رئيس اتحاد الكرة السوداني، الذي انتقد أداء الفريق في الدوري. جاء الرد من إدارة الهلال عبر بيان رسمي، حيث أكدت أن الانتقادات غير مبررة وأن الفريق يسعى لتحقيق النجاح رغم التحديات. كما أشار الهلال إلى التزامه بتطوير كرة القدم في السودان ودعم اللاعبين. البيان شدد على أهمية التعاون بين الأندية والاتحاد لتحقيق الأهداف المشتركة، ودعا إلى التركيز على تحسين الأداء بدلاً من الانشغال بالتصريحات. هذه الحرب الكلامية تعكس التوترات الحالية في الساحة الرياضية السودانية، حيث يسعى كل طرف لتأكيد موقفه.

football.title: الهلال السوداني يصنع الحدث و"غربال" على موعد مع المجد - شبكة تواصل الإخبارية
football.summary: الهلال السوداني حقق إنجازًا كبيرًا في مسيرته الكروية، حيث تمكن من الوصول إلى مراحل متقدمة في المنافسات القارية. اللاعب "غربال" كان له دور بارز في هذا النجاح، حيث أظهر مهاراته العالية وأداءه المتميز في المباريات. الجماهير تتطلع إلى المزيد من الإنجازات، مع آمال كبيرة في تحقيق الألقاب. الهلال يسعى لتعزيز مكانته في الساحة الرياضية، ويبدو أن الفريق في طريقه لتحقيق المجد الذي يطمح إليه.

football.title: الهلال السوداني والسويحلي الليبي يقتربان من مجموعات دوري الأبطال - مانكيش نت
football.summary: اقترب فريق الهلال السوداني وفريق السويحلي الليبي من التأهل إلى مرحلة المجموعات في دوري أبطال أفريقيا. جاء ذلك بعد الأداء القوي الذي قدمه الفريقان في المباريات التمهيدية. الهلال السوداني حقق نتائج إيجابية في مبارياته السابقة، مما يعزز فرصه في التأهل، بينما تمكن السويحلي من تقديم عرض قوي في التصفيات. يتطلع كلا الفريقين إلى تحقيق النجاح في المرحلة المقبلة من البطولة، حيث تعتبر هذه المنافسة فرصة كبيرة لإظهار مهاراتهم على المستوى القاري.

football.title: الهلال السوداني والسويحلي الليبي يقتربان من دور المجموعات في دوري ابطال افريقيا - Elsport
football.summary: اقترب فريق الهلال السوداني وفريق السويحلي الليبي من التأهل إلى دور المجموعات في دوري أبطال أفريقيا بعد أدائهما القوي في التصفيات. حيث حقق الهلال السوداني فوزاً مهماً على منافسه في مباراة الذهاب، مما يعزز فرصه في التأهل. من جهة أخرى، قدم السويحلي الليبي عرضاً مميزاً في مباراته، مما يضعه في موقف جيد للتقدم في البطولة. يتطلع كلا الفريقين إلى تحقيق نتائج إيجابية في مباريات الإياب لضمان مكانهما في دور المجموعات، حيث تعتبر هذه المرحلة من البطولة ذات أهمية كبيرة للأندية الأفريقية.

football.title: الهلال السوداني يحسم مواجهة سيداما بونا ويقترب من التأهل الأفريقي - اخبار السودان
football.summary: حقق فريق الهلال السوداني فوزًا مهمًا على سيداما بونا الإثيوبي في مباراة ضمن تصفيات دوري أبطال أفريقيا، مما يقربه من التأهل للمرحلة التالية. انتهت المباراة بفوز الهلال بنتيجة 2-0، حيث سجل الأهداف كل من اللاعب محمد عبد الرحمن واللاعب وليد الشعلة. قدم الفريق أداءً قويًا خلال المباراة، مما ساهم في تعزيز فرصه في المنافسة على اللقب الأفريقي. بهذا الفوز، يواصل الهلال مسيرته الناجحة في البطولة ويعزز من موقفه في المجموعة.

football.title: موعد بث مواجهة الهلال وسيداما والقنوات الناقلة للقاء المرتقب اليوم - موقع رادار
football.summary: تقام اليوم مواجهة مرتقبة بين فريق الهلال وسيداما، حيث ينتظر عشاق كرة القدم هذه المباراة بفارغ الصبر. ستبدأ المباراة في تمام الساعة 8:00 مساءً بتوقيت مكة المكرمة. سيتم بث اللقاء عبر عدة قنوات، منها القناة الرياضية السعودية، بالإضافة إلى منصات البث المباشر على الإنترنت. يُعتبر هذا اللقاء مهمًا للفريقين، حيث يسعى الهلال لتحقيق الفوز لتعزيز موقفه في البطولة، بينما يأمل سيداما في تقديم أداء قوي أمام خصمهم.

football.title: موعد مباراة الهلال السوداني وسيداما كوفي | مبتدا - مبتدا
football.summary: تقام مباراة الهلال السوداني وسيداما كوفي في إطار منافسات دوري أبطال أفريقيا. يُنتظر أن تُعقد المباراة في يوم 15 أكتوبر 2023، حيث يسعى الهلال السوداني لتحقيق الفوز على الفريق الإثيوبي. يُعتبر الهلال من الأندية العريقة في السودان، ويأمل في تقديم أداء قوي أمام سيداما كوفي لتعزيز فرصه في البطولة. المباراة ستُقام على ملعب الهلال في الخرطوم، مما يمنح الفريق ميزة اللعب على أرضه وأمام جماهيره.

football.title: موعد بث مواجهة الهلال وسيداما والقنوات الناقلة للقاء المرتقب اليوم - موقع رادار
football.summary: تستعد جماهير كرة القدم لمتابعة مواجهة الهلال وسيداما اليوم، حيث من المقرر أن تنطلق المباراة في تمام الساعة 8:00 مساءً بتوقيت مكة المكرمة. ستقام المباراة في إطار المنافسات القارية، مما يزيد من حماس المشجعين. يمكن متابعة اللقاء عبر عدة قنوات ناقلة، منها قناة "SSC" التي تمتلك حقوق البث، بالإضافة إلى منصات البث المباشر. يُتوقع أن تكون المباراة مثيرة، حيث يسعى الهلال لتحقيق الفوز وتعزيز موقفه في البطولة.
